description.en: The first of the four dōjō: Temple 1 Ryōzen-ji to Temple 23 Yakuō-ji, 154.5 km along 22 temple-to-temple henro trail relations. The gentlest of the four to pace — no leg between two temples runs longer than 22.7 km, so every day of it can end at a temple. Awa carries the first of the four stages of spiritual progression the pilgrimage maps onto Shikoku's four provinces: awakening.

distanceNote.en: 154.5 km is this section's own walked line — the shortest connected path through its 22 pinned henro trail relations, measured with the repository's own way graph. Its member ways sum to 155.3 km; the difference is the spurs a walked line leaves out. The four dōjō together measure 1,140.9 km, against the pilgrimage's traditional ~1,200 km figure. Modern walked totals range from about 1,140 km (most efficient) to about 1,400 km (with all variant paths).

estimatedDays.note: Derived from this section's 154.5 km at the pace the whole pilgrimage's own declared figures imply — 1,200 km in 30 to 60 days, typically 45, so 20 to 40 km a day and typically 26.7. min and max are rounded up, typical to the nearest day. The four sections come to 31 to 59 days, typically 44.

origin.en: The pilgrimage traces the path of the monk Kūkai (774-835), founder of Shingon Buddhism in Japan. Kūkai practiced asceticism across Shikoku before founding the monastic center at Mount Kōya. The 88-temple circuit was formalized during the Edo period (1603-1868). The phrase 'Dōgyō Ninin' (walking with two) inscribed on the pilgrim's hat signifies that Kōbō Daishi walks with every pilgrim.

description.en: A calligraphy book purchased at Temple 1 (2,000-3,500 JPY). At each temple, monks write the temple name, principal deity, and temple number in calligraphy and apply three red stamps. Cost: 500 JPY per temple (44,000 JPY total). Stamp hours: 7:00-17:00. One book is carried across all four dōjō.
'Walking with Two' — the belief that Kōbō Daishi walks alongside every pilgrim. Inscribed on the sedge hat. The pilgrim is never alone.

Traditional pilgrim outfit: white jacket (hakui, 白衣) symbolizing purity and readiness for death, sedge hat (sugegasa), walking staff (kongōzue) representing Kōbō Daishi himself, stole (wagesa), prayer beads (juzu), and name slips (osamefuda) deposited at each temple.

At each temple: bow at the gate, purify at the water basin, ring the bell, offer incense and candle at the Main Hall, chant the Heart Sutra (Hannya Shingyō), repeat at the Daishi Hall, receive the stamp. The full sequence takes 20-30 minutes per temple.

Charitable gifts from locals to pilgrims — food, drinks, money, or lodging. A deeply rooted tradition in Shikoku. It is customary to accept osettai graciously and give a name slip (osamefuda) in return.

The walking staff is considered an embodiment of Kōbō Daishi. It must be washed and placed in the room before the pilgrim washes. It must never be placed on the ground where it could be stepped over. In historical times, if a pilgrim died, the staff was used as their grave marker.

etiquette.en: Remove shoes before entering temple buildings.
Do not ring the bell when leaving a temple — only upon arrival.
The walking staff must never be used to point or gesture.
Accept osettai graciously, even if you do not need it. Refusing is considered disrespectful to Kōbō Daishi.

relevance.en: The definitive English-language book on the Shikoku pilgrimage. Statler walked the route multiple times and documented its history, culture, and personal meaning.
Translations of Kūkai's major philosophical and religious writings. Essential for understanding the spiritual foundation of the pilgrimage.

historicalSignificance.en: The Shikoku pilgrimage is one of the few circular pilgrimages in the world and the most important Buddhist pilgrimage in Japan. It embodies the Shingon Buddhist concept of spiritual progression through four stages: awakening, discipline, enlightenment, and nirvana — mapped onto the four provinces of Shikoku.

notes.en: Open year-round but rainy season (June-July) and typhoon season (August-September) are challenging. Winter walking is possible but some mountain temples may be difficult to access. Peak seasons are spring (cherry blossoms) and autumn (fall foliage).

accommodationNotes.en: Shukubo (temple lodging): 6,000-8,500 JPY with meals. Minshuku: 5,500-7,500 JPY with meals. Business hotels: 3,000-8,000 JPY without meals. Cash is essential — credit cards rarely accepted at traditional lodging. Advance reservations recommended.

cellularNotes.en: Good coverage in towns and along main roads. Weak or no signal on mountain trails.

waterNotes.en: Vending machines are ubiquitous in Japan, even in rural areas.

notes.en: Nearest airport to Temple 1. Bus to Naruto/Bando area.
Trains circle most of Shikoku. Useful for reaching temples or skipping difficult sections. JR passes available.

sources.notes: The day divisions are cut by rule rather than taken from a guidebook, so they can be re-run. The rule: a day ends at a temple whenever one falls between 25 and 30 km along this section's route.main.geojson; where no temple does, it ends at the nearest named accommodation or town waypoint on the line instead. Two tie-breaks make it deterministic. Where several candidates qualify the day ends at the one nearest 27.5 km, the middle of the band, and where two are equally near, at the earlier one along the line — the same test in both arms. The fallback arm is not confined to the band, because it exists for the stretches where the band is empty. "Named" means the waypoint carries a name that is a non-empty string other than the literal "Unnamed" the enrichment writes when OpenStreetMap gave the node none: accommodation is not one of the types enrichment requires a name for, so two unnamed accommodation waypoints sit in this pilgrimage's files and the rule filters them itself. A candidate counts as on the line when it lies within 500 m of it, the radius build-ways snaps a stage boundary across. Position along the line is measured by perpendicular projection onto route.main.geojson, not read from a waypoint's own kmFromStart, which this pilgrimage records on two different scales. Section boundaries override both arms: a boundary day ends at the boundary temple itself whatever its length, and the lodging fallback does not apply there. shikoku-88-sanuki holds Temple 88 fixed the same way, so the circuit's closing return from it to Temple 1 is one stage. The spec's original rule was temples only, and the temple spacing does not carry it. Of the 88 temple-to-temple legs, measured on these same lines, only 4 fall inside 25-30 km, while 10 exceed 30 km and carry 552.3 km — 48% of the 1,140.9 km circuit — the longest Temple 37 to Temple 38 at 82.7 km. Across those ten there is no temple to end a day at in either direction, which is what the second arm is for; without it half the route could not be paced at all. Cut 2026-09-09 against the walked line measured the same day. This section came to 5 stages, the four dojo to 40. Each stage's distanceKm is the length of route.main.geojson between its own two anchors, rounded to one decimal, and each anchor's own note records which arm chose it.

osm.note: 22 relations, one per temple-to-temple leg from Temple 1 to Temple 23, in walking order. The Overpass query above is pilgrimage-wide and returns all 89 四国遍路 relations; each section pins the slice of that result it walks. A boundary relation belongs to the section that walks it, so 22番札所~23番札所 (13692105) is here and Awa ends at Temple 23, where shikoku-88-tosa begins. Relation 13669296, 四国遍路 16番札所観音寺~18番札所恩山寺, 19.08 km, is deliberately excluded rather than missing: it is an alternative that skips Temple 17, passing no closer than 1,295 m to Ido-ji against 48 m to Temple 16 and 8 m to Temple 18. The circuit's own path, 16→17 (2.89 km) plus 17→18 (18.12 km), runs 21.00 km, so the alternative saves 1.92 km by leaving a temple out. The pilgrimage visits all 88 temples in order.
